title: Milk Operation and Farm Management (Upcoming Exam)
subtitle: Breeds, Digestion, Feed Nutrients, Silage, Farm Tools, Anatomy, Milking Equipment, Diseases, Terminology & Daily Routine Schedules
instructions: Section I covers Different Breeds of Dairy Cattle (identification and multiple choice).
Section II covers the Digestion Process of Ruminants, including draggable sequence cards for digestion stages and stomach compartments.
Section III covers Basic Feed Nutrients in dairy cattle rations.
Section IV covers Silage Making, including draggable sequence cards for bag and bunker ensiling procedures.
Section V covers Farm Tools and equipment used in dairy operations.
Section VI contains an interactive anatomical diagram identifying the 23 body parts of dairy cattle.
Section VII contains an interactive mechanical diagram identifying the 10 components of the portable milking machine.
Section VIII covers Common Diseases of Calves, Heifer and Cow, including prolapse management resequencing.
Section IX covers Definition of Terms across dairy farming, calving, and digestive physiology.
Section X contains the Dairy Square Daily Routine Time Quiz matching 13 scheduled time windows to the routine diagram.
Section XI contains the Dairy Square Daily Routine Activity Quiz matching 13 daily farm tasks to the routine diagram.
Identification inputs accept forgiving text: casing and punctuation differences are automatically resolved.
Resequencing cards can be reordered by dragging or using the Move Up / Move Down buttons.

sections.title: Different Breeds of Dairy Cattle
sections.description: Characterization of Bos taurus vs. Bos indicus and specifications of primary temperate and tropical dairy breeds.

questions.question: Scientific name of the temperate cattle species characterized by having no humps, short legs, a broad rump, and highly developed milk production:
questions.explanation: Bos taurus cattle originate from temperate countries, are humpless, and are characterized by highly developed milk production.

questions.question: Scientific name of the tropical cattle species known for prominent humps, long legs, a sloping rump, heat resistance, and tolerance to diseases and parasites:
questions.explanation: Bos indicus (zebu) cattle are widely distributed in tropical regions, possess a prominent hump, and have natural tolerance to heat and parasites.

questions.question: Dairy cattle breed originating from the Netherlands with distinctive black-and-white markings, the largest body weight (680–770 kg), and the highest annual milk yield (10,220 kg/year):
questions.explanation: Holstein Friesian originates from the Netherlands and produces the highest milk yield of any dairy breed (10,220 kg/year).

questions.question: Smallest dairy cattle breed (400–450 kg) originating from Jersey Island, France, with a light brown coat and the highest milk fat content (4.8%), making its milk best used for cheese:
questions.explanation: Jersey cattle weigh 400–450 kg, produce milk with 4.8% fat and 3.7% protein, and are prized for cheesemaking.

questions.question: Dual-purpose (milk and beef) dairy breed originating from Switzerland with brown to light-gray markings that resists extreme solar radiation and yields ~9,900 kg milk/year:
questions.explanation: Brown Swiss originates from Switzerland, serves dual-purpose milk and beef production, and withstands extreme solar radiation.

questions.question: Tropical zebu dairy breed originating from Gujarat, India, characterized by a mottled red, yellow, and white coat, heat resistance, and tolerance to tropical diseases:
questions.explanation: Gyr (or Gir) originates from Gujarat, India, and is well-adapted to tropical conditions with good udder conformation.

questions.question: Which dairy cattle breed originates from the Isle of Guernsey, France, has yellow to reddish-brown and white markings, produces 4.7% milk fat, and is noted for being a very efficient converter with calving ease?
questions.explanation: The Guernsey breed originates from the Isle of Guernsey, France, with 4.7% milk fat and a docile temperament.

questions.question: Which dual-purpose breed from Great Britain has white and roan markings, a body weight of 640–680 kg, and a high protein-to-fat ratio (4.0% fat, 3.5% protein)?
questions.explanation: Dairy Shorthorn originates from Great Britain and is used for both milk and beef with a high protein-to-fat ratio.

questions.question: Which breed originates from the County of Ayr, Scotland, features red and white markings, produces 7,700 kg/lactation, and is noted for strong legs, vigorous calves, and being free from genetic disease?
questions.explanation: Ayrshire originates from County of Ayr, Scotland, produces 7,700 kg milk per 305-day lactation, and possesses strong legs.

questions.question: How does the Red & White Holstein differ in desirable characteristics from the black-and-white Holstein Friesian according to the module?

options.A: Red & White Holstein has a strong immune system and is resistant to heat, whereas Holstein Friesian is not resistant to heat and is susceptible to diseases
options.B: Holstein Friesian has a stronger immune system and higher heat tolerance than Red & White Holstein
options.C: Red & White Holstein is the smallest dairy breed, weighing only 350 kg
options.D: Both breeds have identical heat tolerance and disease resistance

questions.explanation: The Red & White Holstein possesses a strong immune system and heat resistance, unlike the black-and-white Holstein Friesian.

questions.question: Which tropical dairy breed from Pakistan and India (weighing 350 kg and yielding 3,500 kg milk/year) has reddish-brown to deep red markings and is specifically highlighted for tick resistance, heat tolerance, and disease resistance?
questions.explanation: Red Sindhi originates from Pakistan and India, yields 3,500 kg milk/year, and has notable tick and heat resistance.

questions.question: Which tropical dairy breed originating from Pakistan and India weighs 425 kg, yields 4,000 kg milk/year, and is prized for good maternal traits, high resistance to parasites, and a well-developed udder?
questions.explanation: Sahiwal cattle originate from Pakistan & India, produce 4,000 kg milk/year, and possess high parasite resistance.

sections.title: Digestion Process of Ruminants
sections.description: Sequential steps of ruminant digestion, stomach compartment anatomy, and lower tract absorption.

questions.question: Arrange the chronological steps of the ruminant digestion process in the correct order from initial feed gathering to final lower tract absorption:

items.text: Prehension and Mastication — Gathering feed using the tongue and lips and chewing into smaller particles
items.answer: Prehension and Mastication — Gathering feed using the tongue and lips and chewing into smaller particles
accepted_answers: Prehension and Mastication — Gathering feed using the tongue and lips and chewing into smaller particles

items.text: Swallowing — Rapidly swallowing feed through the esophagus guided by the tongue (saliva contains no enzymes)
items.answer: Swallowing — Rapidly swallowing feed through the esophagus guided by the tongue (saliva contains no enzymes)
accepted_answers: Swallowing — Rapidly swallowing feed through the esophagus guided by the tongue (saliva contains no enzymes)

items.text: Rumen and Reticulum Fermentation — Microbial digestion in the paunch and particle sorting/trapping at the rumen-reticulum junction
items.answer: Rumen and Reticulum Fermentation — Microbial digestion in the paunch and particle sorting/trapping at the rumen-reticulum junction
accepted_answers: Rumen and Reticulum Fermentation — Microbial digestion in the paunch and particle sorting/trapping at the rumen-reticulum junction

items.text: Rumination (Cud-Chewing) — Regurgitating partly digested cud back to the mouth while resting to re-chew and re-swallow
items.answer: Rumination (Cud-Chewing) — Regurgitating partly digested cud back to the mouth while resting to re-chew and re-swallow
accepted_answers: Rumination (Cud-Chewing) — Regurgitating partly digested cud back to the mouth while resting to re-chew and re-swallow

items.text: Omasum and Abomasum Processing — Grinding feed particles and absorbing moisture in the book, followed by gastric juice digestion in the true stomach
items.answer: Omasum and Abomasum Processing — Grinding feed particles and absorbing moisture in the book, followed by gastric juice digestion in the true stomach
accepted_answers: Omasum and Abomasum Processing — Grinding feed particles and absorbing moisture in the book, followed by gastric juice digestion in the true stomach

items.text: Intestinal Absorption — Absorbing proteins, fats, and carbohydrates in the small intestine and water in the large intestine
items.answer: Intestinal Absorption — Absorbing proteins, fats, and carbohydrates in the small intestine and water in the large intestine
accepted_answers: Intestinal Absorption — Absorbing proteins, fats, and carbohydrates in the small intestine and water in the large intestine

questions.explanation: The ruminant digestive cycle proceeds from prehension/mastication to swallowing, rumen/reticulum microbial fermentation, rumination/regurgitation, omasum grinding/abomasum enzymatic digestion, and intestinal absorption.

questions.question: Arrange the four stomach compartments of a ruminant in the exact anatomical order through which ingested feed passes:

items.text: Rumen ("Paunch" — first and largest compartment lined with millions of papillae)
items.answer: Rumen ("Paunch" — first and largest compartment lined with millions of papillae)
accepted_answers: Rumen ("Paunch" — first and largest compartment lined with millions of papillae)

items.text: Reticulum ("Honeycomb" — pouch-like network that traps foreign objects and collects small particles)
items.answer: Reticulum ("Honeycomb" — pouch-like network that traps foreign objects and collects small particles)
accepted_answers: Reticulum ("Honeycomb" — pouch-like network that traps foreign objects and collects small particles)

items.text: Omasum ("Book" — heavy, hard organ with many internal leaves/folds that grinds feed and absorbs moisture)
items.answer: Omasum ("Book" — heavy, hard organ with many internal leaves/folds that grinds feed and absorbs moisture)
accepted_answers: Omasum ("Book" — heavy, hard organ with many internal leaves/folds that grinds feed and absorbs moisture)

items.text: Abomasum ("True Stomach" — glandular compartment that secretes gastric juices)
items.answer: Abomasum ("True Stomach" — glandular compartment that secretes gastric juices)
accepted_answers: Abomasum ("True Stomach" — glandular compartment that secretes gastric juices)

questions.explanation: Feed flows anatomically from the Rumen to the Reticulum, then into the Omasum, and finally through the Abomasum.

questions.question: The first and largest part of the stomach of ruminants.
A pouch-like structure with tissues forms a network like a honeycomb.
The third stomach compartment, nicknamed the "book", which is a heavy, hard organ with many folds or leaves that grinds feed particles further and absorbs moisture:
questions.explanation: The omasum ('book') has multiple muscular laminae (leaves) that grind feed and extract water.

questions.question: It is also called as "true stomach".
It is where water primary absorbed.
A major site for metabolism of nutrients.
In which part of the lower digestive tract are proteins, fats, and carbohydrates that leave the abomasum primarily absorbed?
questions.explanation: Proteins, fats, and carbohydrates leaving the abomasum are primarily absorbed in the small intestine.

questions.question: Which accessory digestive organ secretes buffers and enzymes directly into the small intestine?
questions.explanation: The pancreas secretes digestive enzymes and buffers into the small intestine.

questions.question: How does the saliva of ruminants differ from that of monogastric (non-ruminant) animals during initial feeding and swallowing?

options.A: Ruminant saliva contains high concentrations of salivary amylase to break down fiber
options.B: Ruminant saliva does not contain digestive enzymes, and ruminants swallow feed rapidly without chewing it adequately at first
options.C: Ruminant saliva is strongly acidic to sterilize forages before entering the rumen
options.D: Ruminants do not produce any saliva until rumination begins

questions.explanation: Ruminant saliva lacks digestive enzymes; feed is swallowed rapidly during initial eating and chewed thoroughly later during rumination.

questions.question: What is the primary function of the rumen-reticulum junction in the ruminant stomach?

options.A: To secrete hydrochloric acid and gastric enzymes into the omasum
options.B: To permanently store ingested hardware and stones
options.C: To prevent large feed particles from passing through to the 3rd chamber and help push food back to the esophagus for rumination
options.D: To absorb water and concentrated minerals

questions.explanation: The rumen-reticulum junction prevents coarse particles from entering the omasum and assists in pushing cud back to the esophagus.

sections.title: Basic Feed Nutrients
sections.description: Proteins, minerals, water, vitamins, fats, carbohydrates, and dietary requirements in dairy nutrition.

questions.question: It is the basic feed nutrients essential for maintenance, growth, and milk production.
It is the basic feed nutrients needed for bone and teeth formation, hormone actions, enzyme activation and water every day.
It is the basic feed nutrients required in the largest amount by the dairy cow.
Nutrients that are organic compounds needed in minute amounts that are essentials for life.
Nutrients that added to the diets to increase energy density. Energy contents are 2.25 times greater than carbohydrates?
It is the common source of energy in ruminants.
These are the building blocks of cow's life.
How many times greater is the energy content of fats compared to carbohydrates in cattle diets?
questions.explanation: Fats provide 2.25 times more energy density than carbohydrates.

questions.question: How much water does a lactating dairy cow require each day at minimum, and how should it be provided?

options.A: 20 to 30 liters; twice daily after milking
options.B: 45 to 50 liters; restricted to morning feedings
options.C: 85 to 90 liters; provided ad libitum (freely available)
options.D: 150 to 200 liters; only mixed with molasses

questions.explanation: A lactating dairy cow requires at least 85–90 liters of water daily, provided ad libitum.

questions.question: Under normal conditions, which vitamins are synthesized by microorganisms in the rumen of dairy cattle?
questions.explanation: Rumen microorganisms synthesize vitamins K and B-complex under normal physiological conditions.

questions.question: Which vitamin is necessary for the absorption and metabolism of calcium and phosphorus, and can be formed as cholecalciferol (D3) by solar irradiation of the skin?
questions.explanation: Vitamin D is essential for calcium and phosphorus regulation and can be synthesized in skin exposed to sunlight.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly pairs a Macro mineral with a Micro mineral in dairy cattle nutrition according to the module?

options.A: Macro mineral: Calcium; Micro mineral: Cobalt
options.B: Macro mineral: Iron; Micro mineral: Phosphorus
options.C: Macro mineral: Zinc; Micro mineral: Magnesium
options.D: Macro mineral: Copper; Micro mineral: Sodium

questions.explanation: Calcium is classified as a macro mineral, while Cobalt is classified as a micro mineral.

questions.question: Arrange the steps of the Hand Method (Squeeze Test) used to estimate chopped forage moisture prior to ensiling:

items.text: Take a handful of freshly chopped forage directly from the harvest
items.answer: Take a handful of freshly chopped forage directly from the harvest
accepted_answers: Take a handful of freshly chopped forage directly from the harvest

items.text: Squeeze the handful of forage firmly in your palm for 20 to 30 seconds to form a ball
items.answer: Squeeze the handful of forage firmly in your palm for 20 to 30 seconds to form a ball
accepted_answers: Squeeze the handful of forage firmly in your palm for 20 to 30 seconds to form a ball

items.text: Release palm pressure and inspect the physical behavior and cohesion of the forage ball
items.answer: Release palm pressure and inspect the physical behavior and cohesion of the forage ball
accepted_answers: Release palm pressure and inspect the physical behavior and cohesion of the forage ball

questions.question: During silage fermentation, sugars present in the fodder are converted into which organic acid that acts as a natural preservative and fermentable energy source for rumen microbes?
questions.explanation: Anaerobic bacteria convert plant sugars into lactic acid, which preserves the silage and lowers pH.

questions.question: What is the recommended standard cut size (in inches) when chopping Corn or Napier forage for silage making?
questions.explanation: Chopping forage to 3/4 to 1 inch facilitates tight compaction and optimal anaerobic fermentation.

questions.question: At every how many inches of added chopped forage is it best to compact the silage during bag filling to remove trapped air?
questions.explanation: Compacting every 3 inches ensures that air pockets are completely eliminated.

questions.question: What is the ideal moisture content of harvested forage for silage making, and what hand-squeeze result confirms it is ready to be ensiled?

options.A: 40%–50% moisture; the ball shatters instantly into dust
options.B: 50%–60% moisture; water drips continuously from the fingers
options.C: 65%–75% moisture; the squeezed forage ball slowly falls apart upon release
options.D: 80%–90% moisture; the ball stays tightly compressed without breaking

questions.explanation: Forage at 65%–75% moisture slowly falls apart upon release, indicating readiness for ensiling.

questions.question: When is prepared silage ready for feeding at a minimum, and how many days of curing produce optimum fermentation as a rule of thumb?

options.A: Ready in 7 days; 14 to 21 days for optimum fermentation
options.B: Ready in at least 3 weeks (21 days); 60 to 70 days produces optimum fermentation
options.C: Ready in 45 days; 120 days for optimum fermentation
options.D: Ready immediately after sealing; 30 days for optimum fermentation

questions.explanation: Silage is usable after 21 days, but 60 to 70 days produces optimum lactic fermentation.

questions.question: Which set of characteristics describes Good Quality Silage compared to Bad Silage?

options.A: Color: bright, light green-yellow or green-brown; Texture: breaks slowly into two when tightly squeezed; Odor: sweet-sour pleasant smell
options.B: Color: dark green to dark brown; Texture: water drips continuously; Odor: putrid or manure smell
options.C: Color: jet black with white mold; Texture: shatters into dry dust; Odor: strong ammonia smell
options.D: Color: pale white; Texture: greasy slime; Odor: rancid butter smell

questions.explanation: Good silage is light green-yellow to green-brown, breaks slowly into two when squeezed, and has a pleasant sweet-sour aroma.

questions.question: Which of the following is a recommended practice when feeding silage to dairy cattle and maintaining stored silage?

options.A: Introduce silage rapidly in full rations on day one, and leave feed bunks uncleaned
options.B: Slowly introduce silage to the animals, clean feed bunks after feeding to prevent spoilage, re-seal opened silage, and repack bags with holes
options.C: Mix silage with wet manure to stimulate bacterial activity, and stack bags uncovered outdoors
options.D: Allow animals to walk over sealed silage bags to maintain compaction

questions.explanation: Gradual diet introduction, cleaning feed bunks, re-sealing storage faces, and repairing bag punctures prevent contamination and spoilage.

sections.description: Infectious, metabolic, reproductive, and parasite disorders in calves, heifers, and adult dairy cows.

questions.question: Arrange the steps in the Management of Pelvic/Uterine Prolapse in the correct clinical sequence:

items.text: Replacement of the prolapsed organ back into its normal position
items.answer: Replacement of the prolapsed organ back into its normal position
accepted_answers: Replacement of the prolapsed organ back into its normal position

items.text: Apply a hypertonic salt or sugar solution to reduce tissue swelling
items.answer: Apply a hypertonic salt or sugar solution to reduce tissue swelling
accepted_answers: Apply a hypertonic salt or sugar solution to reduce tissue swelling

items.text: Suture the vulva (retention sutures) if necessary to prevent re-prolapse
items.answer: Suture the vulva (retention sutures) if necessary to prevent re-prolapse
accepted_answers: Suture the vulva (retention sutures) if necessary to prevent re-prolapse

questions.explanation: Prolapse management consists of organ replacement, osmotic swelling reduction (salt/sugar), vulva retention suturing, and medical therapy.

questions.question: A common disease in calves characterized by swelling of the navel caused by an infection, with pus and transudate leaking from the navel, joint swelling, fever, and death within 5 days in severe cases:
questions.explanation: Navel ill is an infection of the umbilicus in newborn calves; severe cases can cause joint ill and death within 5 days.

questions.question: A severe condition in calves defined as an infection of the blood, presenting with fever, stunted growth, inappetence, lethargy, and sudden death:
questions.explanation: Septicemia is a systemic blood infection that can cause rapid mortality in young calves.

questions.question: A metabolic disorder in dairy cows (medically termed hypocalcemia) caused by a low level of blood calcium within 24 hours or 2–3 days after calving:
questions.explanation: Milk fever (hypocalcemia) occurs shortly after calving due to the rapid drain of calcium into colostrum.

questions.question: The inability of a cow to rise due to muscle and nerve damage caused by prolonged recumbency, slippery flooring ("split cow"), malnutrition, or limb injuries:
questions.explanation: Downer cow syndrome results from prolonged recumbency, nerve compression, or slippery floor trauma.

questions.question: The retention of the fetal membranes for 24–48 hours or more after calving, treated mechanically by manual removal or hormonally with Oxytocin:
questions.explanation: Retained placenta is diagnosed when membranes fail to expel within 24–48 hours of parturition.

questions.question: A reproductive disorder in which one or more organs in the pelvis (vaginal, cervical, or uterine) slip down from their normal position and bulge into or out of the vagina:
questions.explanation: Prolapse involves pelvic organ protrusion (vaginal, cervical, or uterine) through the vulva.

questions.question: Also known as Bovine traumatic reticulopericarditis, this disease is caused by the ingestion of sharp metal or foreign objects that irritate and penetrate the lining of the reticulum:
questions.explanation: Hardware disease occurs when swallowed nails or wire pierce the reticulum wall.

questions.question: Which viral/vector-borne disease of heifers and cows is commonly called "3 days sickness", presenting with fever, drooling, and recumbency followed by recovery after about 3 days?
questions.explanation: Bovine ephemeral fever is known as '3 days sickness' and presents with fever, drooling, and transient recumbency.

questions.question: What are the primary causes and characteristic clinical signs of Calf Diarrhea according to the module?

options.A: Causes: bacterial/viral pathogens, dirty pen/cold weather, bad milk/diet change, stress, and insufficient colostrum; Signs: loose bowel, stained caudal area, dehydration, fever, and lethargy
options.B: Causes: pure vitamin deficiency; Signs: dry cough and blindness
options.C: Causes: high roughage diet; Signs: bloat and constipation
options.D: Causes: excessive milk fat; Signs: hard clods of manure with no fever

questions.explanation: Calf diarrhea results from microbial, environmental, nutritional, and colostrum issues, leading to loose bowel and dehydration.

questions.question: Which clinical sign is specifically noted for Calf Respiratory Problems when the calf is startled or agitated, and what environmental measures help control it?

options.A: Coughing (especially when startled or agitated), labored breathing, and nasal discharge; managed by isolating the sick animal, reducing overcrowding, replacing bedding, proper ventilation, and antibiotic therapy
options.B: Sneezing only during nighttime; managed by restricting fluid intake
options.C: Continuous drooling with high fever; managed by walking through a foot bath
options.D: Loss of horns and hair; managed by spraying cold water

questions.explanation: Agitated coughing, labored breathing, and nasal discharge indicate calf pneumonia, managed with proper ventilation and bedding hygiene.

questions.question: What does the clinical abbreviation LDA stand for in dairy cattle, and what anatomical shift occurs?

options.A: Left Displaced Abomasum — the abomasum shifts from its normal right-ventral position to the left side between the body wall and the rumen
options.B: Lateral Distended Abomasum — the abomasum rotates into the pelvic canal
options.C: Lower Digestive Acidosis — the rumen pH drops below 4.0
options.D: Left Dorsal Atrophy — the rumen wall shrinks due to starvation

questions.explanation: In Left Displaced Abomasum (LDA), the fourth stomach shifts to the left between the abdominal wall and the rumen.

questions.question: Which two specific hoof diseases are highlighted as common causes of lameness in dairy cattle, and how are they managed?

options.A: Foot rot and Inter-digital dermatitis; managed through foot care/trimming and a medicated foot bath
options.B: Navel ill and Septicemia; managed by oral electrolytes
options.C: Sole fracture and Hip dislocation; managed with body harnesses
options.D: Laminitis and Bloat; managed with trocarization

questions.explanation: Foot rot and inter-digital dermatitis cause lameness and are managed via trimming and medicated foot baths.

questions.question: What preventive device is administered orally to cattle to attract swallowed nails and wires and prevent Hardware Disease?
questions.explanation: A permanent cylindrical rumen magnet placed in the reticulum captures ferromagnetic hardware.

questions.question: How are cattle parasites classified on Page 58 of the module?

options.C: Internal parasites (Ticks only) and External parasites (Tapeworms only)
options.D: All parasites are classified exclusively as blood protozoa

questions.explanation: Endoparasites include roundworms, tapeworms, and protozoa; ectoparasites include ticks.

sections.title: Definition of Terms
sections.description: Essential terminology of dairy husbandry, calving, rumination physiology, and milk production.

questions.question: Partly digest food returned from the first stomach of ruminants to the mouth for further chewing.
It is the process by which the cow regurgitates previously consumed feed and chews further?
Is the chewing and grinding of food into smaller particles?
Is the act of gathering food using the tongue and lips and moves it into the mouth?
It is so called cow's "passport to life"?
It is the abnormality or difficulty in giving birth of cow.
It is the act of giving birth.
It is an act of separating the calf attachment from the mother.
A branch of agriculture that encompasses the breeding, raising and utilization of dairy animals for the production of milk and various dairy products processed from it:
questions.explanation: Dairy farming or dairying encompasses breeding, raising, and utilizing dairy livestock for milk production.

questions.question: A large pendulous organ consisting of two or more mammary glands enclosed in a common envelope and each provided with a single teat:
questions.explanation: The udder is the pendulous mammary organ containing the mammary glands and teats.

questions.question: The technical term defined in the Calving and Calf Management module for a newborn animal:
questions.explanation: A neonate is a newborn animal in need of immediate post-natal airway and colostrum care.

questions.question: The normal physiological process in cows of returning partly digested feed from the stomach to the mouth for further chewing:
questions.explanation: Regurgitation is the reverse movement of cud from the stomach to the oral cavity during rumination.

questions.question: According to the Definition of Terms on Page 42, what is Lactation, and what is the standard duration of the Lactation period after calving?

options.A: Lactation is the process of making milk; the standard lactation period is 305 days
options.B: Lactation is the period of pregnancy; the standard duration is 285 days
options.C: Lactation is the process of rumination; the standard duration is 60 days
options.D: Lactation is the dry period; the standard duration is 365 days

questions.explanation: Lactation is milk synthesis and secretion; the standard dairy lactation cycle is 305 days.

questions.question: According to the Definition of Terms on Page 42, what is Gestation, and what is its standard duration in dairy cattle?

options.A: Gestation is the period of time between conception and birth; standard is 285 days
options.B: Gestation is the time between calving and peak milk; standard is 305 days
options.C: Gestation is the period of estrus; standard is 21 days
options.D: Gestation is the weaning duration; standard is 60 days

questions.explanation: Gestation is the pregnancy duration between conception and birth, averaging 285 days in cattle.

questions.question: How much colostrum ("passport to life") must be given to a newborn calf within the first two hours of life, and what antiseptic is used to dip the navel?

options.A: 2 litres of colostrum within the first 2 hours of life; povidone iodine for navel disinfection
options.B: 500 ml of colostrum within 24 hours; isopropyl alcohol for navel dipping
options.C: 5 litres of whole milk; hydrogen peroxide for navel dipping
options.D: 1 litre of water; chlorhexidine for navel dipping

questions.explanation: Calves require 2 litres of antibody-rich colostrum within 2 hours of birth and navel dipping with povidone iodine.

questions.question: What is the definition of Silage making according to Page 33 of the module?

options.A: A method of conserving animal feed by fermenting forage crops (such as Corn and Napier) for times when less animal feed is available
options.B: Sun-drying green grass until moisture drops below 10% to make dry baled hay
options.C: Boiling corn kernels into a concentrated mash for dry cows
options.D: A chemical treatment using urea to dissolve tough crop residues

questions.explanation: Silage making is feed conservation through anaerobic fermentation of forage crops into lactic acid.
